newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Delegates say break-up of E. Timor meeting scary.
newsitem.headline: Delegates say break-up of E. Timor meeting scary.

text.p: An Australian and a Japanese deported by Malaysia for attending a conference on East Timor said on Sunday they were scared and feared there would be a bloodbath when screaming Malaysian youths broke up the meeting.

Andrew McNaughtan, 42, and Ihiro Kimura, 21, flew into Manila on Sunday after they and 14 other activists were expelled by Malaysian authorities, who had refused to sanction the meeting for fear of harming ties with Indonesia.
Indonesia invaded East Timor in 1975 and annexed it the next year in a move never recognised by the United Nations.

They said the meeting on Saturday in a Kuala Lumpur hotel had just begun when members of a Malaysian youth group allied to Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's ruling coalition stormed in and broke it up. Malaysia denied it had backed the intruders.
"They ran amuck, overturning chairs...and screaming...They were extremely threatening," McNaughtan told Reuters.
"I was frightened, very frightened...Really a spark at any moment (and) it could have turned into a bloodbath...It was very frightening because these people were quite irrational."
McNaughtan, convenor of the Australia East Timor Association in New South Wales, added: "It's pretty frightening when you are confronted with a couple of hundred people who are just crazy."
The Manila Times newspaper, one of whose reporters attended the Kuala Lumpur meeting, slammed the incident in an editorial titled "Shame, shame, shame".

"Barbaric," the Times said. "Malaysia certainly is no stranger to strong-arm tactics by its government. But its residents have reason to be appalled by their government's lack of civility toward a harmless, human rights conference."
It said Malaysia "chose a brutal way of sending its message across the world: that it does not tolerate views contrary to its own."
McNaughtan and Kimura said people in charge of conference security tried to prevent the Malaysian youths from getting in but they eventually smashed down one of the doors.

"There was a while I feared there might be violence," Kimura said. "I was very tense at one time...because there was a lot of yelling, a lot of verbal threats, and so I was very intimidated at first." But there was, in the end, no violence.
Kimura said the incident appeared to be "very well orchestrated".

"They came in, tore down all the banners," he said. "There may have been some looting, things were strewn across. We were in the middle of the floor trying to hold the circle. We were being yelled at from behind, from the front."

The Philippine government recently barred the entry of Nobel peace laureate and East Timor resistance leader Jose Ramos-Horta who had been invited to attend a conference being organised by non-governmental groups in parallel with the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum summit on November 25.
Indonesian President Suharto is among leaders to attend the APEC summit.
McNaughtan said he was still weighing his decision on whether or not to attend the counter-summit in Manila.
"I certainly don't want to be deported again. Once is enough."
